relearning.title: Read: reading chemical formulas
relearning.description: A short reading with the combo-meal analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can read a chemical formula and tell what elements are in a compound and how many atoms of each.**

**Think of a combo meal.** One combo is a burger and 2 fries. If the sign says (burger + 2 fries) × 3, you get 3 burgers and 6 fries, because the 3 multiplies everything in the combo. A chemical formula works the same way: parentheses are a combo, and the small number outside them multiplies the whole combo.

**Rule 1.** Each capital letter starts a new element symbol. Na is sodium (one element), not N plus a.

**Rule 2.** A **subscript** (the small number below) counts only the symbol right before it. No subscript means 1. In H₂O there are 2 H and 1 O.

**Rule 3.** A subscript **outside parentheses** multiplies everything inside. In Ba(OH)₂, the 2 doubles both the O and the H.

**Worked example:** Ba(OH)₂. Ba has no subscript, so Ba = 1. O = 1 × 2 = 2. H = 1 × 2 = 2. Total = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 atoms.

checks.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of H₂O?
checks.explanation: The subscript 2 follows H, so there are 2 hydrogen atoms. O has no subscript, so there is 1 oxygen atom.

checks.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in Ca(OH)₂? Type a number.
checks.explanation: The 2 outside the parentheses multiplies the O inside: 1 × 2 = 2.

sections.title: Coefficients and bigger formulas

body.text:
**Coefficients.** A big number in front multiplies the whole formula. 3H₂O means 3 molecules of water: H = 2 × 3 = 6 and O = 1 × 3 = 3. Always multiply, never add.

**Worked example 2:** (NH₄)₂CO₃. The outside 2 multiplies N and H: N = 1 × 2 = 2, H = 4 × 2 = 8. C and O are outside the parentheses: C = 1, O = 3. Total = 2 + 8 + 1 + 3 = 14 atoms.

**Worked example 3:** 2Al(NO₃)₃. First count one formula unit: Al = 1, N = 1 × 3 = 3, O = 3 × 3 = 9. Then the coefficient 2 doubles everything: Al = 2, N = 6, O = 18. Total = 26 atoms.

**Same total does not mean same substance.** H₂O and CO₂ both have 3 atoms, but they are made of different elements, so they are different substances.

**Watch out for:** counting only inside the parentheses and forgetting the outside subscript, adding numbers instead of multiplying (3 + 2 = 5), using a coefficient on only the first element, and reading a two-letter symbol like Ca or Mn as two elements.

checks.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in Cu(NO₃)₂?
checks.explanation: There are 3 O inside the parentheses, and the outside 2 doubles them: 3 × 2 = 6. Adding (3 + 2 = 5) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: How many total atoms are in 2NaCl? Type a number.
checks.explanation: One NaCl has 2 atoms (1 Na and 1 Cl). The coefficient 2 doubles the whole formula, so there are 4 atoms.

sections.shortAnswer: In 2Na₃PO₄, explain what the 2 in front does and what the 3 below does.

checks.prompt: In CO₂, what does the 2 count?

options.text: Both the carbon and the oxygen atoms

checks.explanation: A subscript counts only the symbol right before it, so the 2 counts oxygen. CO₂ has 1 C and 2 O.

checks.prompt: Which of these is ONE element symbol?
checks.explanation: A new element starts at each capital letter. Ca (calcium) has one capital letter. CO and NO each have two capitals, so each is two elements.

checks.prompt: In 3H₂O, what does the 3 do?

options.text: It counts only the hydrogen atoms
It multiplies every atom in the formula
It adds 3 atoms to the formula

checks.explanation: A coefficient multiplies the whole formula: 3H₂O is 3 molecules of water, so 6 H and 3 O.

body.problem: Count every atom in one formula unit of (NH₄)₃PO₄.

steps.text: List the elements. Each capital letter starts one: N, H, P and O.
Inside the parentheses there is 1 N and 4 H. The outside 3 multiplies both: N = 1 × 3 = 3 and H = 4 × 3 = 12.
Outside the parentheses, P has no subscript, so P = 1. O has the subscript 4, so O = 4.

checks.prompt: Your turn: how many H atoms are in (NH₄)₂SO₄? Type a number.
checks.explanation: There are 4 H inside the parentheses, and the outside 2 doubles them: 4 × 2 = 8.

checks.prompt: How many total atoms are in Mg(OH)₂?
checks.explanation: Mg = 1. The outside 2 doubles O and H: O = 2 and H = 2. Total = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5.

relearning.title: U3.LT1 Watch: counting atoms in formulas

checks.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in Al₂(SO₄)₃?
checks.explanation: The 3 outside the parentheses multiplies everything inside, like (burger + 2 fries) × 3: O = 4 × 3 = 12. Adding (4 + 3 = 7) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: How many total atoms are in one formula unit of CaCO₃? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Ca has no subscript, so Ca = 1. C = 1. The 3 counts only the O right before it, so O = 3. Total = 1 + 1 + 3 = 5.

sections.title: Counting atoms with coefficients and subscripts

checks.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 4NH₃?
checks.explanation: One NH₃ has 3 H. The coefficient 4 multiplies the whole formula: H = 3 × 4 = 12. Always multiply, never add (3 + 4 = 7).

checks.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in 2Mg(OH)₂?
checks.explanation: One Mg(OH)₂ has 1 × 2 = 2 O. The coefficient 2 doubles the whole formula: O = 2 × 2 = 4.

sections.shortAnswer: In 3Ca(NO₃)₂, explain what the 3 in front does and what the 2 outside the parentheses does.

relearning.title: Read: ionic or covalent?
relearning.description: A short reading with the lunch-money analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can look at a compound and tell whether it's ionic or covalent.**

**Think of lunch money vs. a shared pizza.** If a friend hands you a dollar, the dollar moves from them to you: one gives, the other takes. That is an **ionic** bond. If you and a friend split a pizza, nobody gives it away; you both eat from it. That is a **covalent** bond. Metals are the "givers" and nonmetals are the "takers." When two takers meet, neither will give, so they share.

**Rule 1.** Metal + nonmetal makes an **ionic** compound: the metal **transfers** electrons to the nonmetal. Metals sit **left of the staircase** on the periodic table. Transition metals like iron and copper are metals too.

**Rule 2.** Two nonmetals make a **covalent** compound: the electrons are **shared**, and one unit is a **molecule**. Hydrogen is a nonmetal, even though it sits on the left.

**Rule 3.** A compound with a **polyatomic ion** is **ionic**. That includes **ammonium, NH₄⁺**, even though ammonium compounds have no metal. Ammonium plays the part of the metal.

**Worked example:** CaBr₂. Calcium is left of the staircase, so it is a metal. Bromine is right of the staircase, so it is a nonmetal. Metal + nonmetal, so CaBr₂ is **ionic**: calcium transfers electrons to bromine.

checks.prompt: Which compound is ionic?
checks.explanation: Potassium is a metal (left of the staircase) and chlorine is a nonmetal, so KCl is ionic. CH₄ and SO₂ are only nonmetals, so they are covalent. Calling CH₄ ionic because hydrogen sits on the left is the common mistake: hydrogen is a nonmetal.

checks.prompt: Ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl, has no metal, but it has the polyatomic ion NH₄⁺. Is it ionic or covalent? Type one word.
checks.explanation: A compound with a polyatomic ion is ionic, even with no metal. Ammonium plays the part of the metal. Calling it covalent because every atom is a nonmetal is the common mistake.

sections.title: Hard cases and lab evidence

body.text:
**Why atoms bond.** Atoms bond **to be stable**. The **octet rule** says most atoms are stable with **8** outer electrons (hydrogen and helium are the exceptions). Noble gases already have a full outer shell, so they don't bond. A **single bond** shares 2 electrons, a **double bond** shares 4 and a **triple bond** shares 6.

**Worked example 2:** (NH₄)₃PO₄ (ammonium is NH₄⁺, phosphate is PO₄³⁻). Every atom is a nonmetal, so the nonmetal rule says covalent... but wait. It has polyatomic ions, and a compound with a polyatomic ion is ionic. Answer: **ionic**.

**Properties are your evidence.** Ionic compounds have **high melting points** (generally above 300 °C), form **crystals** and **conduct electricity when dissolved in water**, because they break into free-moving ions. Covalent compounds have **low melting points**, can be solid, liquid or gas, and **do not conduct** when dissolved, because they stay as whole molecules. Color, mass and where a bottle was stored are **irrelevant evidence**.

**Worked example 3:** An unknown melts at 80 °C and its solution does not light the bulb. 80 °C is far below 300 °C, which points to covalent. No conductivity means no free ions, which also points to covalent. Answer: **covalent**.

**Watch out for:** calling an ammonium compound covalent just because it has no metal, calling hydrogen a metal, calling two metals (like Ca and Mg) ionic, forgetting that transition metals are metals, and using color, mass or "it dissolves" as evidence. Use melting point and conductivity instead.

checks.prompt: An unknown white solid melts at 750 °C, and its solution lights the bulb. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: Ionic: the high melting point and the conductivity both point to ionic
Covalent: it is a white solid

checks.explanation: Melting above 300 °C and conducting when dissolved both point to ionic. Color and dissolving are irrelevant evidence, and using them is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Water, H₂O, is made of hydrogen and oxygen. Is it ionic or covalent? Type one word.
checks.explanation: Hydrogen is a nonmetal even though it sits on the left of the periodic table, so H₂O is two nonmetals: covalent. Calling hydrogen a metal is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why NaCl is ionic but Cl₂ is covalent. Say what the electrons do in each.

relearning.title: Do: flip the rules, then sort the compounds
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a guess-and-flip deck of compounds and lab clues.

cards.back: A metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal. One gives and one takes, like handing a friend a dollar.
Two nonmetals share electrons, like splitting a pizza. One unit is a molecule.
Left of the staircase on the periodic table. Transition metals like iron and copper count too.
A nonmetal, even though it sits on the left. H₂O is two nonmetals, so it is covalent.
A compound with a polyatomic ion, like ammonium (NH₄⁺), is ionic, even with no metal.
Atoms bond to be stable. Most are stable with 8 outer electrons. Noble gases are already full, so they don't bond.

checks.prompt: Which compound is ionic?
checks.explanation: Sodium is a metal (left of the staircase) and fluorine is a nonmetal, so NaF is ionic. CO₂ and PCl₃ have only nonmetals, so they are covalent. Skipping the metal check is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Two chlorine atoms bond to make Cl₂. What happens to their electrons?

options.text: One chlorine transfers electrons to the other
Each atom keeps its electrons, and no bond forms

checks.explanation: Chlorine is a nonmetal, and two nonmetals share electrons: a covalent bond. Transfer happens from a metal to a nonmetal, so picking transfer is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: NH₄NO₃ has no metal (ammonium is NH₄⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻). How should it be classified?

options.text: Covalent, because every atom is a nonmetal
Ionic, because it is made of polyatomic ions
Covalent, because it has three elements

checks.explanation: A compound with a polyatomic ion is ionic, and NH₄NO₃ is made of two of them. Using only the nonmetal rule is the common mistake.

sections.title: Guess, then flip: sort the compounds

cards.back: Ionic. Potassium is a metal and iodine is a nonmetal, so KI is ionic.
Covalent. Both are nonmetals, so SO₂ and SO₃ are covalent: the atoms share electrons.
Ionic. Copper is a transition metal, and transition metals are still metals. CuCl₂ is ionic.
Covalent. Hydrogen is a nonmetal, even though it sits on the left. H₂O is covalent.
Ionic. It is made of polyatomic ions, so (NH₄)₂SO₄ is ionic even with no metal.

cards.front: Unknown A: melts at 801 °C, and its solution lights the bulb
cards.back: Ionic. A melting point above 300 °C and conducting when dissolved both point to ionic.

cards.front: Unknown B: melts at 45 °C, and its solution does not light the bulb
cards.back: Covalent. A low melting point and no free ions both point to covalent.

checks.prompt: Which list has ONLY covalent compounds?
checks.explanation: CO₂, N₂O and CCl₄ are only nonmetals with no polyatomic ion, so all three are covalent. CaO has calcium, a metal, and every compound in the last list starts with a metal. Missing one hidden metal in a list is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved because they break into free-moving ___. Type one word.
checks.explanation: Dissolved ionic compounds break into free-moving ions that carry the current. Covalent compounds stay as whole molecules, so they don't conduct. Saying "electrons" is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: In an ionic bond, what happens to the electrons?

options.text: A metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal

checks.explanation: An ionic bond is like handing a friend a dollar: one gives and the other takes. The metal (the giver) transfers electrons to the nonmetal (the taker). Sharing is a covalent bond.

checks.prompt: Which pair of elements would form an ionic compound?
checks.explanation: Magnesium is a metal (left of the staircase) and oxygen is a nonmetal, so they form an ionic compound. Carbon + oxygen and nitrogen + hydrogen are two nonmetals (covalent). Calcium and magnesium are both metals, so they are not ionic.

sections.title: Ionic or covalent? Deciding from the elements

checks.prompt: Which compound is covalent?
checks.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen are both nonmetals, so NO₂ is covalent: the atoms share electrons. LiF and FeCl₃ have a metal (iron is a transition metal, still a metal), and NH₄Br has the polyatomic ion ammonium, so all three are ionic.

checks.prompt: HCl is made of hydrogen and chlorine. Is it ionic or covalent? Type one word.
checks.explanation: Hydrogen is a nonmetal even though it sits on the left of the periodic table, so HCl is two nonmetals: covalent. Calling hydrogen a metal is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why KBr is ionic but CO₂ is covalent. Use the periodic table, and say what the electrons do in each.
